title: The sticky note for a forgetful genius

beats.say: Imagine a brilliant temp worker who forgets everything each morning. How do you stop explaining the same things every single day?
You leave a one page note on the desk. Claude reads a file called CLAUDE dot md at the start of every session. That file is the note.

chip.text: Read at the start of each session

beats.say: But a note only helps if it is short. Do not write that the temp knows how to use email. Write what only your office knows: odd rules, key commands, and places never to touch.

show.title: What goes on the note
items: Skip: things any expert already knows

beats.say: Every word costs reading effort, called tokens. So a short, specific note beats a long, vague one.

check.q: Which line best earns its place in a CLAUDE.md?
opts: Write clean, readable code
Never read the data/raw folder
Python is a programming language
check.why: It is specific to your project and Claude cannot guess it. The other two are generic or already known.

work: Write down three rules a new teammate would only learn by making a mistake.
Delete any line from your notes that says something every engineer already knows.

title: Where CLAUDE.md lives and how it loads

beats.say: Where does Claude get your rules before you type a single word?

From three places. A CLAUDE dot md in the repo, committed so the whole team shares it. A personal one in your home dot claude folder, applied to every project. And CLAUDE dot md files in subfolders, loaded only when Claude works in that folder.

chip.text: Repo shared, home personal, subfolder on demand

beats.say: Run slash init and Claude explores the repo and drafts one. Drafts tend to be chatty, so cut it down to what is specific and non-obvious.
When one section grows long, import another file with an at sign and its path. And when Claude makes the same mistake twice, add one line.

show.title: CLAUDE.md
show.text:
@docs/data-rules.md
- Late files arrive up to 3 days late.

check.q: You want a rule that applies to you in every project but should not be committed. Where does it go?
opts: ./CLAUDE.md in the repo
~/.claude/CLAUDE.md
A subfolder CLAUDE.md
check.why: The home file is personal and loads for every project. The repo file is shared with the team, and a subfolder file only loads for that folder.

work: Run /init on one repo, then cut the draft by half.
Move one personal preference out of the repo file into your home file.

title: Why a bloated CLAUDE.md backfires

beats.say: Why can a longer CLAUDE dot md make Claude worse, not better?
Because the whole file is loaded into context every session. Fill it with generic advice like write clean code, and the one rule that matters gets buried in noise, while you pay tokens every time.
Specific beats obvious. EU amounts use a decimal comma, twelve comma fifty, while US uses thousands commas. Claude cannot guess that trap. PEP 8 it already knows.

show.title: Keep vs cut
items: Keep: late files up to 3 days
Cut: PEP 8 and what pandas is

beats.say: Watch the gotchas. Stale rules that contradict the code. Secrets pasted in, when the file is committed, so name the variable, never the value. And it is guidance, not enforcement.

check.q: Which is the best reason to remove a line saying follow PEP 8?
opts: Claude already knows it, so it only costs tokens
PEP 8 is outdated
Claude cannot read style rules
check.why: Lines that restate common knowledge add cost and dilute the rules that matter.

work: Audit your CLAUDE.md for stale commands by running each one.
Search it for tokens or passwords and replace values with variable names.

title: What belongs in CLAUDE.md, and what does not

beats.say: A rule in CLAUDE dot md is a request, not a lock. So what should live somewhere else?
Hard guarantees, like never reading dot env, need enforcement: permission settings or hooks that block the action. Keep the line in CLAUDE dot md only to explain why.
Long procedures used rarely belong in skills or slash commands, loaded on demand instead of paid for every session. Subfolder files keep payments rules out of the data team's context.

show.title: Put it where it is paid for least

beats.say: Treat the file like code. Review it in pull requests, prune it regularly, and add a line only after a repeated mistake. Past a page or two, split it or delete.

show.sub: a page or two, then split or delete

check.q: A rule must never be broken: Claude must not read the .env file. What is the best design?
opts: Write it in capitals in CLAUDE.md
Block it with permission settings or a hook, and explain it in CLAUDE.md
Put it in a skill
check.why: CLAUDE.md is advisory. Only enforcement guarantees the behavior, and the note explains why.

work: List your must-never rules and check each has a permission or hook behind it.
Move any rarely used multi-step procedure from CLAUDE.md into a skill or slash command.

title: Skills: the recipe binder shelf

beats.say: How can an assistant know hundreds of your team's rules without reading them all every single time?

show.text: Hundreds of rules, one short memory

beats.say: Think of a kitchen with a shelf of recipe binders. The chef does not read every recipe before cooking. Each binder has a label on the spine saying when to use it.

chip.text: Only the spine label is read

beats.say: When a customer orders a cake, the chef spots the baking label, and only then opens that binder.
A skill works the same way. It is a folder with instructions inside. Claude sees only the short label until the task matches. That keeps its memory light.

show.title: A skill in one line
items: Full text loads when the task matches

check.q: In the binder analogy, what does Claude read before a task matches a skill?
opts: Every full recipe
Only the label on the spine
Nothing at all
Only the last page
check.why: Only the short name and description sit in context. The full instructions load when the task matches, which keeps sessions lean.

work: List three rules your team repeats in code reviews; each could become a skill.
Pick one and write a one-line label saying when it applies.

title: How a skill loads, step by step

beats.say: What actually happens when you ask Claude to write a pipeline test, and a skill kicks in?

show.text: Ask for a test. A skill appears.

beats.say: A skill is a folder under dot claude slash skills, with a file called skill dot m d. At the top are two fields: a name and a description. Those two lines are all Claude loads at session start, maybe fifty tokens per skill.

You ask for a loader test. Claude compares your request to every description, finds that data checks matches, and then reads the full body. Rules like: load the same day twice, expect the same row count.

show.title: From request to rules
items: You ask for a loader test
Rerun test: same day twice, same rows

beats.say: The folder can also hold scripts, which Claude runs without pasting their code into context.

check.q: What sits in Claude's context from the start of a session for each skill?
opts: The full SKILL.md body
Every script in the folder
Just the name and description
Nothing until you type a slash command
check.why: Only the name and description are loaded up front. The body loads when the description matches the task.

work: Create .claude/skills/data-checks/SKILL.md with a name, a description and three numbered rules.
Ask Claude to write a loader test and check whether it follows your rules.

title: Why your skill never fires

beats.say: Your skill exists, but Claude never uses it. Why?

show.text: The skill is there. Claude ignores it.

beats.say: Matching runs on the description alone. A line like, helpful data stuff, gives Claude nothing to match. Write when to use it: when writing or reviewing pipeline tests or data quality checks.

show.title: Descriptions say *when*
items: Strong: use when writing or reviewing pipeline tests
Name the task and the trigger words
Claude matches on this line only

beats.say: The opposite fails too. A broad description fires on every task and loads the body for nothing, burning context. Fifty overlapping skills also compete, and the wrong one may win.
Remember the split. Rules needed every session belong in CLAUDE dot m d. Rules needed only sometimes belong in a skill. And a script in the folder runs with your permissions, so review it like code.

check.q: A skill for pipeline tests never loads. What is the most likely fix?
opts: Make the body longer
Rewrite the description to say when to use it
Move the folder into the data directory
Add more skills with similar text
check.why: Claude matches on the description. A vague one never matches, so state the task and trigger conditions.

work: Audit every skill description: does it say when to use it, in task words?
Merge or sharpen skills whose descriptions overlap.
Read any bundled script before committing it.

title: Skills vs hooks, CLAUDE.md and commands

beats.say: Can a skill guarantee your data checks actually run?

show.sub: Think before you rely on it

beats.say: No. Loading is the model's choice, so it is probabilistic. A rule that must never be skipped, like blocking negative amounts in production, belongs in a CI test or a hook that always runs.
Use skills for judgment and know-how: house style, how we write checks. Use CLAUDE dot m d for a few always-true facts, and a slash command when a human wants to trigger a routine on purpose.

show.title: Pick the right tool
items: CLAUDE.md: a few facts, always loaded
Slash command: a human triggers it
CI or hook: must never be skipped

beats.say: Keep skills in the repo, review them in pull requests, and give each an owner. Stale advice spreads quietly. Test them by running real tasks and seeing whether the skill loads.

show.title: Treat skills like code
items: Run real tasks to test loading

check.q: Which rule is best enforced in CI or a hook instead of a skill?
opts: Our preferred naming style for test files
Never write negative amounts to production tables
How to structure helper functions
Tips for explaining pipeline failures
check.why: A must-never-break rule needs deterministic enforcement. Skills are loaded at the model's discretion, so they suit guidance, not guarantees.

work: Split your rules into must-enforce, which go to CI or hooks, and guidance, which goes into skills.
Add an owner and review step for each skill folder.
Test each skill with three realistic prompts and record whether it loaded.

title: A kitchen that never forgets

beats.say: Imagine hiring a brilliant cook who forgets everything each morning. How do you avoid re-explaining your kitchen every day?
First, a rules poster on the wall. The cook reads it before every shift. That is CLAUDE dot M D. It holds standing facts, like how to run tests and which freezer never to open.
Second, a recipe card with a name on it. You say the name, and the cook follows the card. That is a slash command: a saved instruction you start yourself, by typing a slash and its name.
Third, a cookbook shelf. The cook reads the spine labels and pulls down the right book when a job needs it. That is a skill. Claude decides when to use it, not you.

check.q: In the kitchen analogy, which layer is the cookbook the cook chooses from the shelf without being told?
opts: CLAUDE.md
A slash command
A skill
check.why: A skill is picked by Claude when its description fits the job. CLAUDE.md is always read, and a slash command runs only when you type it.

work: List three things you keep re-explaining to an AI assistant in your data repo.
Label each one as always-true rule, task you start, or know-how Claude should spot.

title: What loads, and when

beats.say: Your project has three kinds of knowledge. Which one is loaded every single time, and which waits to be called?

CLAUDE dot M D is read automatically at the start of every session. So every line costs attention every time. Keep it short: build command, test command, conventions, and what not to touch. Aim for under two hundred lines.
A slash command is a markdown file in a commands folder. The file name becomes the command. Type slash review and its text is sent as your prompt. It costs nothing until you call it.

A skill is a folder with a SKILL dot M D file and optional scripts. At start Claude sees only its name and description. If your task matches, it loads the full instructions. So the description decides whether it ever fires.

check.q: You want Claude to follow your dbt test style whenever it edits models, without you asking. Which layer fits best?
opts: A slash command named dbt-tests
A skill with a clear description
A longer README
check.why: A skill is loaded when Claude judges the task relevant from its description. A slash command needs you to remember to type it.

work: Check the length of your CLAUDE.md and trim anything that is not needed every session.
Turn one prompt you paste weekly into a command file in the commands folder.

title: Why the rule got ignored

beats.say: Why does Claude sometimes ignore a rule you clearly wrote down?

show.sub: Usually a layer problem, not a model problem

beats.say: Often the file is too long. CLAUDE dot M D loads every session, so a three hundred line file buries the key rules. Also it is guidance, not a lock. If breaking a rule would be dangerous, enforce it with permissions or a hook.
Skills fail quietly. A vague description like helps with data never matches, so the skill never loads. Write it with trigger words: use when writing or editing dbt tests.

show.title: Chance a skill fires, by description
items: use when writing or editing dbt tests

beats.say: Slash commands fail differently. Nobody runs them if nobody remembers they exist. And never put secrets in any of these files, because they live in git where everyone can read them.

show.title: Two more traps
items: Unknown commands never get run, so list them in CLAUDE.md
Secrets in these files are readable by everyone with repo access

check.q: A rule that must never be broken, such as no writes to production tables, is in CLAUDE.md but was violated once. What is the best fix?
opts: Write the rule in capital letters
Enforce it with permissions or a hook
Move it into a slash command
check.why: CLAUDE.md is guidance that Claude weighs. Permissions and hooks run outside the model's judgment, so they actually block the action.

work: Rewrite every skill description to start with use when and name the exact trigger.
Move any must-never rule into permissions or a hook, and scan these files for secrets.

title: Choosing the right layer

beats.say: You have one piece of knowledge. Which layer owns it? Choose wrong and you pay in tokens or in missed runs.

show.sub: Wrong choice costs tokens or missed runs

beats.say: Ask two questions. Should it apply every time? Then CLAUDE dot M D, but only if it is short. Who starts the work? If you do, make a slash command. If Claude should notice, make a skill.
Move long procedures out of CLAUDE dot M D into skills, so you pay for them only when used. Point to existing docs instead of copying them, because copies drift.

And know the limits. Anything that must happen exactly, like blocking a production deploy, belongs in CI, hooks or permissions, not in prose. Treat all three layers as code: review them in pull requests.

show.title: Limits and governance
items: Must-happen controls go in CI, hooks or permissions
Prose guides judgment; it does not guarantee behavior
Version and review all three layers like code

check.q: Your CLAUDE.md has a 90 line backfill procedure that is needed twice a month. What do you do?
opts: Leave it, since the model needs it
Move it into a skill or slash command
Delete it and rely on memory
check.why: A rarely needed procedure in CLAUDE.md costs attention in every session. A command or skill loads it only when it is used.

work: Audit CLAUDE.md and move any rarely used procedure into a skill or command.
Put all three layers in git and require pull request review for changes.

title: A recipe card for your AI

beats.say: What if your best code review lived on a card that every teammate could pull out with one word?

show.sub: A saved card anyone can use

beats.say: Think of a recipe card in a shared kitchen binder. The card has a name on the tab. Anyone says the name, and the cook follows the same steps, every time.
A slash command works the same way. You save your instructions in a plain text file. The file name becomes the command. Type slash review-pipeline, and Claude follows your card.
Put the binder in the project folder and share it. Now the whole team gets the same careful review, not one person's mood that day.

show.title: Why share the binder
items: Improve the card once, all benefit

check.q: What makes a saved slash command useful for a team?
opts: It makes Claude faster at thinking
Everyone runs the same saved instructions with one short name
It hides the prompt from teammates
check.why: The value is consistency: one shared file means every person runs the same review instead of writing their own prompt.

work: Pick one prompt you retype often and write it down as a file.
Ask a teammate to run it and compare their result with yours.

title: From Markdown file to slash command

beats.say: How does a text file turn into a command you can type?
Claude looks in the folder dot claude slash commands. Every Markdown file there becomes a command named after the file. Save review-pipeline dot md, and you get slash review-pipeline.

Whatever you type after the command replaces the placeholder called dollar ARGUMENTS. Type slash review-pipeline pipeline slash load dot py, and the prompt now says review that exact file. The at sign tells Claude to read the file.

show.title: Placeholder swapped in
show.text:
Review @$ARGUMENTS as a senior data engineer.

/review-pipeline pipeline/load.py
=> Review @pipeline/load.py ...

beats.say: The top block, called front matter, holds a description. It shows in the command menu so teammates know what it does. Commit the folder to git and everyone shares it.

check.q: You run /review-pipeline pipeline/load.py. What happens to $ARGUMENTS?
opts: It is replaced by pipeline/load.py in the prompt
It is ignored and the file runs as code
It is replaced by the command's description
check.why: The text typed after the command is substituted for the placeholder, so the prompt targets that exact file.

work: Create .claude/commands/ and add one command with a clear description.
Use $ARGUMENTS with an @ so the target file is attached.
Commit the folder so teammates get it on their next pull.

title: Why your command gave a vague answer

beats.say: Your command ran, but the review was vague. Why?

show.text: A command is only a prompt

beats.say: A command is just a prompt. Claude can still wander, so the file must pin down the output. Do not edit is a request, not a lock. Cap findings at ten, and demand file and line plus a failing input. Without limits you get an essay.

Gotchas. If you type no argument, the placeholder becomes empty, and the prompt reads review nothing. Name the target clearly or ask for a file. Also, a list of checks is only as good as its list: idempotency, late data, string-built SQL, secrets in logs.
And do not paste real secrets or customer data into the file. It is committed, so everyone can read it forever.

check.q: A command says Do not edit. What does that guarantee?
opts: Claude cannot write files
Nothing; it is an instruction, and permissions are what enforce it
The file becomes read only on disk
check.why: The text steers behavior but is not a safeguard. Real limits come from tool permissions.

work: Add a required-argument line so an empty call asks for a file.
Rewrite one vague command to demand file:line and a failing input.
Scan your command folder for secrets or real data.

title: When a slash command is the wrong tool

beats.say: Should every team habit become a slash command?

show.sub: Choose the right home for each rule

beats.say: No. A command runs only when someone remembers to type it. Rules that must always hold, like never log PII, belong in CLAUDE dot md, or in a CI check that blocks the merge.

Commands fit repeatable tasks with a human trigger: reviews, release notes, backfill plans. Each one costs tokens, since the whole file plus the files it references load into context. Keep them short and focused.

show.title: Good fits for commands
items: Short and focused, tokens cost money

beats.say: Pick skills when the work needs scripts or many steps loaded on demand. Version commands like code, review changes, and retire stale ones, or the team's trust drifts.

check.q: Which rule is best enforced in CI rather than only in a slash command?
opts: Draft release notes for this sprint
Never commit secrets to the repo
Review load.py when asked
check.why: A command depends on someone running it. A rule that must always hold needs automatic enforcement.

work: List your team's rules and mark which must always hold; move those to CI or CLAUDE.md.
Trim any command that references many large files.
Assign an owner to review the commands folder each quarter.
